passage: I'm Sachin, and I sit across from Kashish in the data team. The new joiner, Tanmay, had spent his first month saying 'All good!' to everything, even when his reports came back covered in red. Last Thursday Kashish pulled her chair over to his desk. I couldn't help overhearing. She told him about her first year, when she'd sent a wrong forecast to the whole regional office and hid in the washroom for twenty minutes. Then, quieter, she explained which managers actually read the reports and which only read the summaries. Tanmay laughed for the first time I'd heard. On Monday he walked up to her and said, 'Honestly, I'm lost on the pricing model.' I can't know what changed inside him, but something did.

qa.q: How long did Kashish hide in the washroom after the wrong forecast?
qa.a: She hid in the washroom for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Tanmay's honest "I'm lost on the pricing model" suggest about how he felt after the talk?
qa.a: It suggests he felt less alone and safer admitting struggle, because his senior had shown her own mistakes first.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's approach work better than simply telling Tanmay to ask for help?
qa.a: By sharing a real failure and honest details about who reads what, she showed candour first, which made it easier for him to be candid back.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the change in Tanmay?
qa.a: He noticed Tanmay laughing and then asking openly for help, and senses something shifted, though he admits he can't know what happened inside him.

grounding: A colleague watches a senior woman share an early failure and honest office-politics details, after which a new joiner becomes more candid.

passage:
Week one. Zubin kept his sketches hidden until they were perfect, and when Ritu asked how the site plan was going, he said, "Fine, almost done," three days running.
Week two, Wednesday. Over chai in the studio kitchen, Ritu told him about her first project, a clinic whose staircase she'd drawn one metre too short. "The contractor spotted it. I wanted the floor to swallow me." Lowering her voice, she added that the partners care more about deadlines than beautiful drawings, and that she'd learned it the hard way.
Week three, Monday. Zubin put a messy, half-finished plan on her desk. "The parking doesn't work and I don't know why. Can we look together?" Ritu pulled up a stool.

qa.q: What had Ritu drawn one metre too short?
qa.a: She had drawn a clinic's staircase one metre too short.

qa.q: What does Zubin's messy half-finished plan in week three suggest about how he now feels?
qa.a: He seems less afraid of looking imperfect and more willing to be honest, trusting that Ritu won't judge him for mistakes.

qa.q: Which choice by Ritu built the rapport, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her own staircase mistake and a frank detail about what the partners value made her human, so Zubin felt safe to bring problems early.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu had only talked about her successes?
qa.a: Zubin would probably keep hiding his work until it was perfect, missing help and deadlines, because the gap between them would feel too big.

grounding: Over three weeks a senior architect shares an early failure and an honest note on office priorities, and her mentee begins to share problems openly.

passage:
"Can I tell you about my first year here?" Dilnaz stirred her tea. "I lost the biggest client in the building."
"You? No way."
"I sent the wrong contract. Cried in the stairwell. My manager then didn't speak to me for a week."
Ishita laughed, then covered her mouth. "Sorry."
"Laugh, it's funny now. Also, since we're being honest, the monthly review isn't about numbers only. The director likes people who explain problems early. Nobody tells you that."
Ishita put her cup down. "Can I be honest too? I've been hiding a delay on my project because I was scared."
"Good. Let's fix it together."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz send by mistake in her first year?
qa.a: The wrong contract.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz share her own failure with Ishita?
qa.a: She wanted Ishita to feel less alone and safe enough to be honest, showing she cared about building trust.

qa.q: What turning point does this conversation create for Ishita?
qa.a: She admits the hidden project delay, and can now fix it with help before the monthly review.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita to hear that a senior once cried in the stairwell?
qa.a: It seems to relieve her and make her feel less alone, which is why she finally admits being scared.

grounding: Shows a senior sharing her early failure and honest details about office politics, which lets the mentee be candid.

passage:
When Aditi joined my team, she was so polished it worried me. Every answer perfect, every slide perfect. I recognised it. As a young woman in this firm, I'd done the same.
So over lunch one day I told her about my first performance review, the one where my boss wrote "lacks judgement" and I spent the weekend applying for other jobs. I told her which meetings actually decide things and which are theatre, and that Mr Rao remembers who interrupts him.
Aditi went very still. Then she said, "I've been pretending I understand the budget process. I don't."
I laughed. "Nobody does in their first year." After that, Zeenat and Aditi weren't just boss and junior. We were two people working things out.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's boss write in her first performance review?
qa.a: "Lacks judgement."

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she saw how polished Aditi was?
qa.a: She felt worried, because she recognised the same pressure to seem perfect that she had felt as a young woman in the firm.

qa.q: What made Zeenat's approach work at this stage?
qa.a: She shared a real failure and honest details about which meetings matter, which made it safe for Aditi to admit what she didn't understand.

qa.q: What is it like for Aditi to hear Zeenat's story?
qa.a: It seems to relieve her pressure to look perfect, so she can admit something she was hiding.

grounding: Shows a senior sharing her early failures and honest office details, making her mentee feel less alone and more candid.

passage:
Mentoring note, week three
I noticed Lalremsiami keeps saying "all good" in our check-ins, even when her deadline slips. So today I changed my approach. When I was a new girl in this office, I missed a launch date so badly that the whole team stayed until midnight. I told her that story, and also that our department head reads emails late at night but hates getting them after nine, which nobody writes down anywhere.
She laughed properly for the first time. Then she said her dataset has been broken for two weeks and she was scared to say. We made a plan for it on the spot. I will keep sharing my mistakes when they help.
Binita, team lead

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami keep saying in check-ins?
qa.a: "All good."

qa.q: Why did Binita decide to share her own missed launch?
qa.a: She was concerned that Lalremsiami felt too scared to admit problems and hoped an honest story would help her feel less alone.

qa.q: What did Binita's honesty make possible, and what should she keep doing?
qa.a: Lalremsiami admitted the broken dataset, so they could plan a fix; Binita should keep sharing her mistakes when they help.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami have been feeling during the two weeks she said nothing?
qa.a: She was probably anxious and alone, afraid that admitting the broken dataset would make her look bad.

grounding: Shows a senior's note on sharing her early failure and office politics, which helps the mentee admit a hidden problem.

passage:
Wednesday night
Coffee with Vijay today, our third. He's twenty-two, sharp, and so worried about looking stupid that he never asks anything in meetings. So I told him about my first year here: the client deck I sent with the wrong company's logo on every slide, and crying in the stairwell afterwards. His eyes went wide. "You?" I also told him, honestly, that Ramesh in finance says yes in meetings and no over email, and that it's not personal. Vijay laughed properly for the first time. Then he admitted he had been stuck on the vendor report for a week and was scared to say so. That's the first real thing he's told me. I think sharing my disasters did more than any advice. Note to self, Tenzin: keep being honest, and keep the gossip kind.

qa.q: What mistake was in Tenzin's client deck in the first year?
qa.a: The wrong company's logo was on every slide.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose to share the stairwell story?
qa.a: Tenzin wanted Vijay to feel less alone and less afraid of looking stupid, and was glad when it helped him open up.

qa.q: What does this stage show about how rapport is built?
qa.a: Honest stories of struggle, plus a few frank tips about how people behave at work, made Vijay candid enough to admit he was stuck.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay to hear that Tenzin once cried in the stairwell?
qa.a: Vijay is surprised and relieved, laughing properly for the first time and feeling safe enough to confess about the vendor report.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague sharing early failures and honest details of office politics, which helps a junior feel less alone and more candid.
